tip: 'Chez' plus a person means at their place: 'il est resté chez lui' = he stayed at his home. There's no single English word for it.
'Garder les enfants' means to babysit, literally to keep the children: 'elle a gardé les enfants de sa voisine'.
'Tout le monde' literally means all the world, but it just means everyone: 'elle a dit bonjour à tout le monde' = she said hi to everybody.
You 'walk' the dog with 'promener': 'tu as promené le chien'. It means to take out for a walk – you're walking it, not strolling yourself.
'Faire les courses' isn't running races – here 'courses' means errands, and 'faire' (to make/do) covers shopping: 'tu as fait les courses' = did you do the shopping.
French weather mostly runs on 'faire': 'il faisait froid' is literally 'it was making cold'. Heat works the same way – 'il fait chaud'.
'En fait' means 'actually, in fact'. Don't reach for the false friend 'actuellement' – that one means 'currently'.
Some verbs of motion use 'être' in passé composé: 'elle est arrivée'. The past participle agrees with the subject ('arrivée' = feminine).
French usually uses the plain article for body parts, not 'their': 'elles ont ouvert les yeux' = they opened the eyes, meaning their own. Ownership is understood.
'L'' replaces 'le/la' before a vowel or silent 'h': 'l'hôtel', 'l'aéroport'. This shortening is required, not optional.
'S'attendre à' means to expect, not to wait – it carries a 'se' pronoun plus 'à': 'je ne m'attendais pas à ce résultat' = I didn't expect this.
The imparfait sets the scene, the passé composé breaks it: 'dinaient' was the ongoing dinner, 's'est eteinte' the sudden moment the light died.
'On' is the everyday stand-in for 'you/one/people in general': 'on entendait' = you could hear. It always takes the 'il/elle' verb form.
'Chercher' already includes 'for': 'je cherchais un restaurant' = I was looking for a restaurant. Never add 'pour' after it.
'Voulais' is the ongoing wish (I wanted to), 'a fermé' the one event that killed it – passé composé for what suddenly happened.
With 'avoir', the past participle ignores the subject – 'elles ont adoré' stays 'adoré', never 'adorées', even for an all-female crowd.
'Répondre' needs 'à' before the thing answered: 'tu réponds à mon message' = you reply to my message. Don't drop the 'à'.
'Tomber' takes 'être', not 'avoir': 'il est tombé' = he fell. Falling counts as a change of place, so it swings to 'être' like 'aller' and 'venir'.
'Neuf' means brand-new, never used: 'chaussures neuves' are fresh out of the box. 'Nouveau' just means new-to-you, so a used car can be 'ma nouvelle voiture'.
No word for 'on' with days: 'vendredi' alone means on Friday. Add 'le' – 'le vendredi' – and it flips to every Friday.
'Toute la journée' = all day. 'Tout' agrees with the noun: 'tout le temps', 'toute la nuit'.
After 'quelque chose', an adjective needs 'de': 'quelque chose d'intéressant' = something interesting. Same with 'rien' and 'quelqu'un': 'rien de bon'.
To pass an exam is 'réussir un examen' – literally to succeed it. 'Réussir' often takes 'à', but with a test it can go direct: 'réussi ton examen'.
'Appuyer' needs 'sur' to mean press: 'appuyer sur le bouton'. You press on the button, not the button itself.
'Travailler dur' uses the bare adjective 'dur' as its adverb, not 'durement'. A handful of verbs do this: 'parler fort', 'coûter cher'.
'Commencer' links to a following verb with 'à': 'commencé à apprendre'. The preposition is fixed – you memorize 'à' vs 'de' per verb.
Reported speech shifts the tense back: 'il a dit qu'il était désolé' = he said he was sorry. The imparfait 'était' stands in for a present 'je suis désolé'.
Prefer one thing to another with 'à': 'le chocolat au café' ('au' = 'à' + 'le'). French says preferred-to, never preferred-than.
'Visiter' is for places: 'visiter un musée'. For people, use 'rendre visite à': 'rendre visite à un ami'.
'Promettre' attaches a following verb with 'de': 'promis de revenir'. Compare 'commencer à' – there's no logic, each verb just picks 'à' or 'de'.
